{{Short description|American mathematician}}
'''Edward Charles Posner''' (August 10, 1933 – June 15, 1993) was an American [[information theory|information theorist]] and [[neural network]] researcher. He became chief technologist at the [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]], and founded the [[Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems]].

==Education and career==
Posner was born on August 10, 1933, in [[Brooklyn]], and graduated from [[Stuyvesant High School]] in 1950; at Stuyvesant, one of his close friends was mathematician [[Paul Cohen (mathematician)|Paul Cohen]].<ref name="nips"/>
He took only two years to complete his undergraduate studies in [[physics]] at the [[University of Chicago]], graduating in 1952, and he then switched to [[mathematics]] for a master's degree in 1953 and a PhD in 1957.<ref name="nips"/><ref name="e+s">{{citation|title=Edward C. Posner 1933–1993|department=Obituaries|journal=Engineering and Science|publisher=[[California Institute of Technology]]|volume=56|issue=4|date=Summer 1993|page=44|url=http://calteches.library.caltech.edu/623/02/Obituaries.pdf}}.</ref> While a graduate student, he also visited [[Bell Labs]], and later claimed that he had been assigned to the desk there that had formerly been [[Harry Nyquist]]'s.<ref name="nips"/> His doctoral thesis, supervised by [[Irving Kaplansky]], was on the subject of [[ring theory]] and entitled ''Differentiably Simple Rings'';<ref>{{mathgenealogy|id=5726}}</ref> at only 26 pages long, it held the record for the shortest doctoral thesis at the university.<ref name="nips"/>

After finishing his studies, he became a mathematics instructor at the [[University of Wisconsin]] and then an assistant professor of mathematics at [[Harvey Mudd College]].<ref name="nips"/><ref name="e+s"/> In 1961, [[Solomon W. Golomb]] hired him to lead the Information Processing Group at JPL.<ref name="nips"/> He led the group for 10 years and then, after a sequence of positions in higher management,<ref name="nips"/> he became chief technologist in JPL's Office of Telecommunications and Data Acquisition in 1982.<ref name="e+s"/> He also held lecturer and visiting faculty positions in the [[applied mathematics]] and [[electrical engineering]] departments of the [[California Institute of Technology]] beginning in 1970.<ref name="nips"/><ref name="e+s"/>

He died after being hit by a truck while bicycling to work on June 15, 1993.<ref name="e+s"/>

==Contributions==
In [[ring theory]], Posner is the namesake of [[Posner's theorem]], stating that certain [[Tensor product of algebras|tensor products of algebras]] with the [[field of fractions|fields of fractions]] of their [[Center (algebra)|centers]] are [[central simple algebra]]s.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Lanski | first = Charles
 | issue = 2
 | journal = Pacific Journal of Mathematics
 | mr = 961236
 | pages = 275–297
 | title = Differential identities, Lie ideals, and Posner's theorems
 | url = http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.pjm/1102689262
 | volume = 134
 | year = 1988| doi = 10.2140/pjm.1988.134.275
 | doi-access = free
 }}.</ref>

Posner's research in [[information theory]] and [[coding theory]] was applied in the design of the [[NASA Deep Space Network]], used for the communications between spacecraft and their base stations on Earth. He also studied [[communications network]]s and [[cellular telephone]] [[Telephone exchange|switching systems]],<ref name="e+s"/> and was an advocate for [[basic research]] in the US space program.<ref name="nips"/>

Beginning in the early 1980s, Posner founded the study of [[neural network]]s at JPL and Caltech, and helped create the interdisciplinary graduate program in [[Computation and Neural Systems]] at Caltech.<ref name="e+s"/> He also helped found the annual [[Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems]], served as general chair of the first conference in 1987, and chaired its oversight body, the NIPS Foundation.<ref name="nips">{{citation|first=Rod|last=Goodman|contribution=In Memoriam: Edward C. Posner 1933–1993|title=Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 6 (NIPS '93)|editor1-first=J.|editor1-last=Cowan|editor2-first=G.|editor2-last=Tesauro|editor3-first=J.|editor3-last=Alspector|publisher=Morgan-Kaufmann|year=1994|pages=xviii–xxv|contribution-url=http://id3490.securedata.net/rod/pdf/RG.Paper.CP67.pdf}}.</ref>
